corrections.workload: Split a generated text of 50,000 space-separated words (3 to 8 lowercase letters, about 325 KB) into words, count frequencies in a hash map, then report the most frequent word and the vocabulary size; 360 timed iterations after 72 untimed warm-up iterations (run.js). A verifier simulation of the suite's LCG gives 18,623 distinct words and a unique top word ('tea', 9 times), reproducing run.js's checksum 1998586832 over 432 runs, so all languages do the same work.
corrections.why_faster: Not stated by the suite; inferred from the sources. Go splits with strings.Fields, whose substrings share the text's backing array (no copies), and counts in the built-in map[string]int (Swiss-table maps since Go 1.24). C++ extracts each word with istringstream operator>> (sentry plus per-character locale checks) into a std::string (the 3-8 letter words fit the small-string buffer, so no heap copy) and inserts into node-based std::unordered_map<std::string,int>, one node allocation per distinct word (about 18,600 per iteration). A standard-library and idiom effect, not code generation.
corrections.caveats: Mostly a standard-library and idiom comparison (tokenizing and hashing containers), so the result is about istringstream and node-based unordered_map, not code generation; a C++ version with string_view keys and a flat hash map would likely close the gap (inference, not measured). Other languages also beat every C/C++ row: Crystal 0.88 s, Zig 0.91 s, Rust 1.021 s, Java/OpenJDK 1.272 s (the Java row is a separate verified record of the same test). The C version (strdup of the whole text every iteration, strtok_r, uthash with a strdup per new key) is slower still at 1.963-2.084 s. LangArena calls itself 'a subjective benchmark' and says AI tools helped translate the tests between languages. The suite publishes one measurement per test and configuration (no variance). The headline C/C++ 'prod' rows are -O2 with hardening flags, but the -O3 Fast, Unsafe and PGO variants were also compared and Go still wins; the Makefiles' -flto flags are link-only, so the 'LTO' builds probably get no LTO. The per-benchmark ratios are derived from the results file, not stated by the suite. Rows were picked by the search agent as text tests where a Rust, Zig or Go production row beats every C and C++ row; most other text tests in the suite go the other way (for example Base64::Encode and Base64::Decode, where C is about 3x faster than Rust, and Distance::Jaro, which is a tie).

notes: Confirm at A: runtimes match the results file row for row (Go 1.129 s, C++/G++ 1.638 s, C++/G++/PGO 1.587 s best, C/Clang 1.988 s, RSS 11.3 MB), metadata checks out (MIT, 41 stars, not a fork, last commit 2026-10-08), and a simulation reproduces the run.js checksum, so the work is identical. Shortcomings to record: standard-library/idiom win (istringstream plus node-per-key unordered_map vs strings.Fields plus Swiss-table map), not codegen; Crystal, Zig, Rust and Java also beat C++; single measurement per configuration; subjective AI-assisted suite; prod C/C++ rows at -O2 (the -O3 rows also lose); LTO flags inert; 1.45x more memory than C++.

The Rust patterns use Unicode-aware \d, \w and \s (the crate's default) while RE2 and PCRE2 without UCP use ASCII classes, so Rust does the more general match. Only 10 timed iterations. corrections.why_faster: Not stated by the suite; inferred from the sources. Rust's std HashMap (hashbrown SwissTable) stores entries inline in one open-addressing array, while libstdc++ std::unordered_map<uint32_t,int> allocates a node per distinct 4-gram, and every string pair builds two maps. Rust wins despite hashing with the default SipHash-1-3 against libstdc++'s identity std::hash<uint32_t>, so the gap is the container layout and per-node allocation, not code generation.
corrections.caveats: Container comparison: a C++ open-addressing map (absl::flat_hash_map, boost::unordered_flat_map) would likely close the gap (inference, not measured), and the suite only uses std::unordered_map. Other languages also beat every C/C++ row: Zig 0.52 s, C#/JIT 0.516 s (a separate verified record of the same test), Go 0.603 s, Julia 0.58 s. The C version (uthash, one malloc per distinct gram) is slower still at 1.789-1.844 s for the non-instrumented Clang/GCC rows.
